text: The mine closed, and the town it existed for stayed where it was. Inside that arithmetic Kira Kovalenko places a young woman and the relatives she loves exactly as much as she needs to get away from them. The film runs 97 minutes and rarely leaves arm's reach of her; affection arrives as supervision, and a hand on the shoulder doubles as a way of knowing where she is. Nothing is announced. Money, a locked door, permission to be somewhere — these get negotiated in half-sentences, in rooms where a third person is always present. Its editor took the European Film Award, and the reason is audible in the cuts: scenes stop a moment before anyone would have justified themselves. North Ossetia is not a backdrop here but a set of distances — how far it is to anywhere else, and how long the walk back takes.

Revenge in a Western is a bookkeeping problem: one man owes, one man collects, and the distance between them is the cost of travel. Jeymes Samuel takes 137 minutes over a transaction that fits in a sentence — Nat Love wants Rufus Buck, and Buck has just been let out of prison. The extra room goes to the gang. Recruitment is the real pleasure here: terms traded in doorways, old grudges priced, a crew assembled for one purpose and visibly carrying other plans. Buck is written as a boss rather than a brute, a man with holdings and employees and a settled sense of what he is owed, which turns the pursuit into something closer to a raid on a business than a chase across country. A Western this long has to make its waiting interesting. The interest is in the company.

A woman from another planet lands on Earth to find a husband and turns up on a mountainside with no men on it. Kim Cho-hee has 28 minutes and spends them on a collision: a science-fiction arrival on one side, on the other the old machinery of a folk tale, in which a deer spared from a hunter owes its rescuers a wish. Soon-shim wants a marriage. Dal-rae is up there gathering wild greens, which is work, not a plot. The pairing turns quieter than the premise sounds — a granted wish forces the question of what either woman would name if she had to say it aloud, and the comedy keeps landing in the gap between the wish available and the wish meant. Short films can afford to be strange rather than complete, and this one takes the allowance.

It takes a while to notice that the women on screen are one woman. Arnaud des Pallières builds Orpheline out of separated stretches of a single life — a young arrival in Paris who comes near disaster, a composed adult who has filed her past under settled business — and leaves the assembling to be done in the watching. The order is not the order in which things happened. That withholding is the method rather than a trick: each section plays as its own small film, with its own weather and its own risk, and the links arrive late enough to alter what the earlier parts meant. 111 minutes, and the tension is largely retrospective, which is a strange thing for a drama to attempt — what accumulates is a person, not a plot.

A Manhattan restaurateur is at ease in a room designed for people who will be leaving. Will Keane has perfected the pleasant, expiring evening, which is why the film starts paying attention the moment he meets a younger woman who treats his practiced self like a costume. Joan Chen keeps the affair on a seasonal clock; the calendar does work the dialogue mostly declines to do. 103 minutes, and the shape is old and unembarrassed about it — two people in a city agreeing to something neither describes accurately to the other. Charlotte is written as the free one, though the freedom looks a lot like refusing to plan. What gives the romance its edge is the asymmetry of habit: he is used to endings that cost him nothing, and this one will not oblige.

An aspiring writer falls in love at first sight, which is the easy part, and then has to live with the person he fell for. Jerry Falk's trouble is not Amanda; it is that he narrates himself faster than he acts, and the film gives him 108 minutes of sidewalk and apartment in which to keep doing it. Woody Allen writes the couple as fluent people: they can describe their situation precisely, from several angles, at length, and the describing is what they do instead of repairing it. The comedy runs on that gap. Amanda is unpredictable in the particular way that keeps a certain kind of man interested and useless, and New York supplies enough rooms to move between that neither of them has to leave first. A romance about postponement, colder than the genre usually permits.

A schoolteacher and a college professor have organised their lives around a child they do not yet have. Malice begins in that ordinary planning — two salaries, a house, appointments kept — and then routes everything through a hospital, where a surgeon with no doubts about himself takes charge of a body that is not his. Harold Becker's picture is less interested in harm than in authority: who gets to make decisions about another person, and how fast a married couple's private arrangement becomes a matter for professionals. 107 minutes, and unusually domestic for a thriller; the menace is procedural, assembled out of confident explanations and the manner of a man rarely contradicted in a room he controls. Andy teaches; Jed operates. Only one of them is used to being obeyed.

The household is a forty-year-old screenwriter, a seventeen-year-old boy and several cats, and money is short. Ahn Seon-kyoung films it from the inside, where the age gap turns out to be only one item on the list of things that make Gaeul unacceptable to her family: they are aggrieved by the cats too, and by the vegetables, and by what a screenwriter earns. The accumulation is the point. Visits and phone calls arrive as a running audit of her life, conducted by people who love her and keep a ledger, while Joseph sits in the middle of it as a fact nobody will address directly. 97 minutes at close range, the days measured in what gets cooked, who pays and which door is shut. Poverty does more damage here than disapproval, and it does it slowly.
